Case A

A1: The search of the past seven days returned only the earlier requests from the one region. The key was published at some point, and the burst came 19 minutes after publication. Nothing in the seven-day window shows misuse before the burst. But the search covers only seven days, and requests could have been missed if the key was published earlier than that or the search was incomplete. The burst is the first misuse seen in the window, but "first misuse of this key" cannot be confirmed from the window alone. Since the publication time is known (19 minutes before the burst) and the window covers publication, requests between publication and the burst would have shown up in the search. The search returned only the earlier ones, so nothing happened in between. Still, "No" is not supported, and "Yes" holds only for the observed logs. I'll say Yes, as the logs show no earlier misuse and the window covers the period since publication.

A2: The check scored the account 30 minutes after publication, when the burst (at 19 minutes) was already available. The shared payout destination was also in the record. The check did not flag it, but we don't know what inputs the check uses or whether those signals were available to it. Cannot tell.

A3: A shared destination does not by itself prove one owner. The answer is "No, not by itself".

A4: No reports after 30 days is weak evidence at best, since victims may not notice or report. The options are "Yes, weakly", "No", and "Cannot tell". The absence of recorded findings does not indicate legitimacy when no one may be looking. "Cannot tell" fits better, since the absence could mean either. I'll choose Cannot tell.

A5: The burst shows a different fingerprint, a residential proxy, and changes to the payout destination, webhook, and schedule right after publication. This warrants investigation: Yes.

Case B

B1: Each account has 100 transactions. D has 0 chargebacks against 2 for the others. D's rate is lower: Yes.

B2: The combined measure is 5 percent, but it includes alerts, and the per-account figures are not given for that measure. A combined figure can hide an account above 5 percent. The answer is No.

B3: The search found no accounts beyond A and the closed account, but it covers only what the search could match, so hidden accounts under other names are possible. The search does not show there are none. The answer is No... The question asks whether the search shows it; it does not. The options are Yes/No/Cannot tell. I'll say No.

B4: Two notes from different analysts on different days could be independent, but we don't know whether the second relied on the first or used the same data. Cannot tell.

B5: A blocked payment is not a completed transaction and has no chargeback because it was stopped. It should not count as non-fraud: No.

B6: Shared templates and descriptor patterns justify investigating together: Yes.

RESULT CN-023 | A1: Yes | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: Yes | B2: No | B3: No | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
